newsitem.title: USA: Northeast says hires nuke whistle-blower.
newsitem.headline: Northeast says hires nuke whistle-blower.

text.p: The head of Northeast Utilities' troubled nuclear operation said Wednesday the company had hired former whistle-blower Paul Blanch to advise on restarting the idled Millstone nuclear plants.

Northeast Nuclear President and Chief Executive Bruce Kenyon also said in a statement that Billie Pirner Garde and James K. Perry, Jr., were joining the independent oversight team for Millstone employee concerns.
Northeast's three Millstone nuclear plants have been closed for safety reasons since March of last year. The company has said all three will be ready for restart by early 1998.
Northeast is also in the process of dismantling its 582-megawatt Connecticut Yankee nuclear plant in Haddam Neck, Conn.
Blanch is a former Northeast employee and whistle-blower who resigned from the company in February 1993.

In the past two years he has worked with other prominent nuclear critics in identifying major design and regulatory deficiencies associated with the storage of spent fuel on nuclear power plant sites.
Kenyon said that the addition of Blanch, Garde and Perry demonstrated Northeast's "commitment and our willingness to submit what we do to critical review."
But anti-nuclear watchdog groups remain deeply skeptical of Northeast despite Blanch's rejoining the utility.

"We're glad Northeast decided to hire back Paul Blanch, one of the most vocal and controversial of the whistle-blowers. But we don't believe it's going to defuse citizens' concerns," said Rosemary Bassilakis, a researcher with Citizens' Awareness Network.
"There's also the issue of the 104 (Northeast) employees who were laid off in January (1996) that hasn't been addressed," Bassilakis told Reuters.
She said some of the laid off workers may have been targetted as people who raised safety concerns.
Northeast has said the layoffs were for economic reasons.
The citizens' groups are equally unhappy with the federal Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC), which is investigating Northeast.
"They've been willing to look the other way and not enforce regulations in order to keep nuclear power an economically viable industry," said Bassilakis.
Bassilakis said she was "somewhat disappointed" that Blanch had agreed to rejoin the utility. "But I don't think he's going to begin to keep his mouth shut. He's a very vocal person."

Blanch told Reuters on Wednesday his role would be to represent the public interest and ensure that the utility complied with regulations in restarting the Millstone plants and dismantling Connecticut Yankee.
